summary: This document extends ABNF, the notation for writing protocol syntax, with a way to specify US-ASCII string literals that are matched case-sensitively. Base ABNF string matching is case-insensitive.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds a clear way to write case-sensitive strings in ABNF. Use %s when uppercase and lowercase letters must match exactly; without a prefix, matching remains case-insensitive.

questions: how to make abnf strings case sensitive
subtitle: ABNF prefixes for writing quoted strings that must match case exactly or ignore case.

tldr.problem: ABNF quoted strings were case-insensitive, so a case-sensitive rule had to list character codes individually.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds the %s prefix for case-sensitive strings and the %i prefix for case-insensitive strings; no prefix keeps the existing case-insensitive behavior.
tldr.outcome: Grammar authors can write case-sensitive US-ASCII literals directly. RFC 7405 updates RFC 5234.

today: RFC 7405 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5234. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why ABNF Needed a Change
sections.content:
Augmented Backus-Naur Form (ABNF) is used to describe protocol syntax. Under RFC 5234, quoted US-ASCII string literals match without regard to case.

When a rule needed case-sensitive matching, authors had to use numeric character values. RFC 7405 adds prefixes so that both case-sensitive and case-insensitive string literals can be written directly.
sections.plainLanguage: ABNF quoted strings used to ignore letter case. The old way to require exact case was to write each character as a number.

sections.title: The %s and %i Prefixes
sections.content:
The prefix %s marks a case-sensitive string, while %i marks a case-insensitive string. A quoted string with no prefix remains case-insensitive, preserving the earlier behavior.

For example, %s"aBc" matches that exact capitalization. A string such as "abc" or %i"aBc" matches regardless of capitalization.
sections.plainLanguage: Use %s when every letter must have the stated case. Use %i, or no prefix, when uppercase and lowercase versions should both match.

sections.title: Updates to RFC 5234
sections.content:
RFC 7405 replaces the discussion of literal text strings in Section 2.3 of RFC 5234 and replaces the char-val rule in Section 4. The new rule permits both case-insensitive and case-sensitive quoted strings.

The RFC says numeric character specifications remain available, but prefixed literal strings are easier to read. Its Security Considerations section says security is believed to be irrelevant to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The update changes two parts of RFC 5234 to allow the new prefixes. Existing strings without a prefix keep their earlier meaning.

data.title: String literal examples
data.code:
%s"aBc" ; matches exactly aBc
%i"aBc" ; matches without regard to case
"abc"     ; same as %i"abc"

references.text: Crocker, D. and P. Overell, "Augmented BNF for Syntax Specifications: ABNF", STD 68, RFC 5234, January 2008.
